items.title: Meta-analysis combines studies — but inherits their flaws
items.claim: Glass and Smith's 1977 meta-analysis pooled psychotherapy outcome studies. What's the standard caveat for any meta-analysis?

options.text: 'Garbage in, garbage out' — if individual studies are biased (publication bias, small samples, poor methods) the meta-analytic average inherits the bias. PRISMA guidelines (2009, updated 2020) standardise reporting; risk of bias assessment is essential

items.reveal:
Funnel plots can reveal publication bias (asymmetry suggests missing small studies with null results). Trim-and-fill methods attempt to correct it. PROSPERO (2011) registers planned systematic reviews.

Cochrane Reviews are widely regarded as the gold standard but even Cochrane has had to retract or revise reviews (e.g., on screening) as methods evolved.
items.why: Meta-analyses summarise evidence but don't fix bias at source. Reading meta-analyses well requires understanding what was included and what wasn't.

items.title: Vygotsky's ZPD emphasised social learning
items.claim: Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development (work in 1920s-30s, popularised in West from 1962 onwards) describes:

options.text: The gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from a more knowledgeable other — emphasising social context as constitutive of cognitive development
A physical region of the brain
A stage of motor development only

items.reveal:
Vygotsky died in 1934 aged 37. His work was suppressed in Stalin's USSR and reached the West in translation (Thought and Language, 1962; Mind in Society, 1978).

'Scaffolding' was Bruner's term (Wood, Bruner & Ross 1976) capturing the temporary support that enables a learner to reach beyond independent ability. Modern educational applications: peer tutoring, guided discovery, gradual release of responsibility models.
items.why: Vygotsky's emphasis on social context contrasts with Piaget's relatively solitary child. Modern developmental psychology integrates both — children develop through cultural participation, not despite it.

items.title: Gage's personality change was real but exaggerated in retelling
items.claim: The story of Phineas Gage (1848) is widely taught as a sudden, permanent personality transformation. What does modern scholarship suggest?

options.text: He was permanently and severely changed forever

Personality changes occurred but Macmillan (2000) and others find evidence of substantial recovery over time; Gage worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile for years, requiring social and planning skills
Gage was unaffected by the injury

items.reveal:
Malcolm Macmillan's 'An Odd Kind of Fame' (2000) compiled the historical record. After his 1848 accident, Gage worked at a livery stable in New Hampshire, then drove a long-distance stagecoach in Valparaiso, Chile (1852-59) — a demanding job requiring planning, social interaction and route management.

He died in 1860 after a series of seizures. The neuroimaging reconstructions of his injury (Damasio et al. 1994, Van Horn et al. 2012) suggest damage to left frontal regions and white matter tracts.

The textbook story ('No longer Gage') exaggerates permanence.
items.why: Iconic case studies become simplified in retelling. The brain's capacity for functional reorganisation matters for both clinical practice and theory.
